TESTIMONY OF
Deirdre Gilbert
Department of Marine Resources

The Department of Marine Resources (DMR) is testifying

O24 1/

in Opposition to

LD 1284- An Act to Offer Military Veterans a 50 Percent Discount on the License Fee

for a Commercial Shellfish License

Before the Committee on Marine Resources

Sponsored by Representative Tuell

Date of Hearing: February 12, 2026

Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Marine
Resources, my name is Deirdre Gilbert, lam Director of State Marine Policy at the Maine Department
of Marine Resources, and lam testifying on behalf of the Department in opposition to LD 1231.

LD 1231 would provide that military veterans honorably discharged would be eligible for a commercial shellfish license at half ofthe cost paid by other commercial shellfish license holders. Certainly the
Department appreciates, and is grateful for, the Veterans who have served our country. For this
reason, the Department has supported providing noncommercial licenses for both lobstering and scalloping to disabled veterans at no cost. This is consistent with what is offered by our sister agency,
Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, who issue complimentary licenses to fish, trap, or hunt to disabled
veterans.

The difference with LD 1231 is that it would provide this discount to all veterans, and for a commercial
endeavor. When we sought feedback from the Shellfish Advisory Council on this bill they declined to
take a vote but generally indicated that they felt that all individuals doing the same commercial activity should have to pay the same license fee.

For additional context, the total cost of a commercial shellfish license for individuals over the age of 18 and under the age of 70 is $133. The license fee for a commercial shellfish license is $58.25, of which $40.75 goes to the General Fund and $17.50 goes to to the Department's dedicated "Opportunity Fund" . There is also a surcharge on this license of $74.75, which goes to the Shellfish Fund. Because
LD 1231 proposes only to offer a 50% discount on the "license fee" , it would lower the cost of this license from $133 to $104. If the proponents intended to also provide a 50% discount on the license
surcharge, it would reduce the cost of the license to $67, which would have a negative effect on the
Shellfish Fund. The impact of that reduction is difficult to estimate, because DMR does not have any
information on the number of veterans holding commercial shellfish licenses.

Finally, individuals fishing commercially for shellfish in towns that have a municipal shellfish
management program are also required to obtain a license from the town. For clarity, LD 1231 would
not impact the fees a veteran must pay for a license issued by the town.

While sincerely appreciative ofthe service to our country, the Department would be concerned that if the precedent were set to issue commercial shellfish licenses to veterans at half the cost, it would be
difficult to explain why all other commercial harvesting licenses are not available to veterans at the same discount. Again, without any information about the number of veterans holding these licenses, there would be an unknown impact to the General Fund, and Department dedicated accounts used for the management and enforcement of these fisheries.
Thank you for your consideration, and I would be happy to answer any questions you might have.

I am Representative Will Tuell, and I am here today to present LD 2031, "An Act
to Offer Military Veterans a 50 Percent Discount on the License Fee for a
Commercial Shellfish License." on behalf of a constituent who sen/ed in the military during the Vietnam War era and came home to little praise or
appreciation.
During my first first term, I submitted a bill that allows young people to purchase
a state clam license for half price. The price of a state license at the time was $133. It may still be, so for Downeast kids who use that money to buy school clothes.and supplies - yes, they still do - the $66 savings was a blessing, and it showed that our state was committed to encouraging young people to get into
the workforce.
That bill also opened the door to young people getting into commercial fishing. Clamming, while not the half billion dollar behemoth, a major part of our
commercial fishing economy. Several of my towns rank among the highest
grossing clamming towns in the state, or have, in recent years.
That bill won unanimous support of the committee at the time and became law. Since, a generation of young clammers have benefited by the savings, some as much as $500-600 over the span of their young lives.
Fast forward to today. This bill seeks to help veterans who have come home -- some from war, some from deployment halfway across the countiy or the world -
by offering them the same deal. A small thank you for their service, and, just as
importantly, something that can help them re-enter the civilian world. For some, it
may be a supplemental income; for all, it is a vote of confidence that you are a contributing member of society.
In these days of affordability being the buzzword, this bill makes it easier for someone who has paid an incredible debt to our society to make ends meet. While $66 doesn't seem like a lot to some, this state has record surpluses and reserve funds, and ought to be able to help people who put their lives in harm's way earn their own way.

House District 10

This is not a handout for veterans. Clamming is back breaking work, and the
numbers of clammers are small. When I talked with Deirdre prior to submitting this bill, she told me there were roughly 1,000 clam diggers statewide.
One of her concerns was that the Department had no way of tracking how many of those 1,000 people are veterans. When l told Representative Strout about this
on one of our white knuckle rides back to Washington County, she suggested
that we could simply change the bill to require proof of honorable discharge.
Representative Thorne has experience in the recruiting field and could likely also
offer up some ideas for how the department could, within existing resources, identify clam diggers who are veterans.
I know that the Department is going to testify against this bill. Their biggest argument, beyond the tracking and quantifying a fiscal note, is what kind of a
precedent this will set for other fisheries. I would argue that fishermen still have to navigate the entry guidelines for all fisheries and that clamming is one of the
smallest. One of the bigger barriers to getting in, that this bill doesn't address, is
the fact that clammers still have to purchase a town license or secure a license through an out of town lottery.
I want to make it clear that I am not suggesting we upset that dynamic or that we
halve municipal shellfish conservation budgets. Towns are struggling to maintain what they have on shoestring budgets, this bill only applies to the state license.
With that though, the entry into each fishery is not apples to apples but apples to oranges, or, in this case, clams to lobsters.
Lastly, to I would say to anyone who believes this is a handout and that veterans
are not expecting a freebie, that it takes a special person to be able to get up at 3 a.m. venture out onto the flats in a howling wind, beat your hoe into the clay, and sack buckets upon buckets of clams back to terra firma all before the tide changes. It's work -- work I can't do and most here, with the exception of Rep.
Simmons and maybe a couple others, haven't done.
I have also included with my testimony a copy of my constituent, Tom Sprague's,
thoughts on this legislation. Please read them, deliberate, and consider supporting a bill that only the most rugged, determined veterans will utilize.
Thank you!
